A recommendations feature starts timing out in production. The runbook says: set

, no restart needed, because the file reloads automatically. Someone makes the change. The endpoint keeps calling the slow service until a restart forty minutes later. The runbook was half right: the file did reload. The service that reads the flag never looked at it again.
The belief is built on true facts.
, so the configuration really does change while the app runs. Reading

directly returns the new value right away. Microsoft's docs demonstrate editing a file and refreshing the page without a restart. And on a developer machine, the app restarts so often that a stale value rarely survives long enough to notice.
What none of that says is when your options object gets rebuilt. That's the part that differs between the three interfaces.
Configuration reloads; options objects are built from it
takes a configuration section and binds it to an instance of your class, such as

. Configuration is the live source; the options object is a copy made at some moment. Whether you ever see a change depends on when that copy is made again, and each interface answers that differently. Reading
directly would always be fresh, but you'd trade typed properties and validation for string keys scattered through the code.
is registered as a singleton. Its

is created on first access and kept for the app's lifetime, so changes made after startup are never read. It also doesn't support named options. That's the right behavior for settings that should only change with a deployment, and it's the cheapest of the three.

is scoped. The options are computed once per request, when first accessed, and stay the same for the rest of that request. That consistency is useful: a request never sees half old and half new settings. The cost is a rebind on every request, which the docs flag as a possible significant performance penalty. And because it's scoped, it can't be injected into a singleton.
returns the latest bound value, and
registers a callback that runs when the source changes. That makes it the only one of the three a singleton can use to follow changes.
; dispose it when the object that registered the callback goes away, or the callback keeps it alive.
Only some sources change at all

Change notifications come from file-based providers such as JSON files and user secrets. Environment variables and command-line arguments are read once at startup, so no interface will ever see a new value from them without a restart.
